power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Existing evidence on co-occurring binge eating and cannabis use is preliminary, and it is unclear how common the combination is or how much burden it carries.
We examined both questions among college students, who are high risk for both behaviors.
Method: We pooled ten annual cohorts (2015-16 to 2024-25) of the Healthy Minds Study (577,962 students, 807 campus-year clusters).
Eating pathology was measured with the SCOFF loss-of-control item.
A subsample of 17,114 students also completed the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q).
Estimates were weighted for non-response and clustered by campus.
Results: Across cohorts, loss of control over eating was reported by 39.0% of past-30-day cannabis users and 30.7% of non-users (adjusted OR = 1.43, p < .001).

text.text: Conclusions: Binge eating is common among students who use cannabis and is more severe at higher frequencies of cannabis use.
Importantly, co-occurrence carried higher odds of depression, suicidality, self-injury, and academic harm.
Thus, these cross-sectional findings underscore the need for dedicated longitudinal research.
Binge eating is characterized by recurrent episodes in which an individual eats an unusually large amount of food and experiences a subjective sense of loss of control over eating.

It is the defining feature of binge-eating disorder (BED) and a core feature of bulimia nervosa (BN) in the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5; Association, 2013), wherein binge episodes in BN are followed by compensatory behaviors (e.g., self-induced vomiting).

text.text: By early adulthood, 5.5% to 17.9% of young women and 0.6% to 2.4% of young men have experienced a DSM-5 eating disorder (Silén & Keski-Rahkonen, 2022).

text.text: Regular binge eating is more common still, and only a minority of individuals who binge eat meet criteria for BED (Keski-Rahkonen, 2021).
text.formatted: Regular binge eating is more common still, and only a minority of individuals who binge eat meet criteria for BED <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Keski-Rahkonen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Binge eating also tends to occur alongside substance use (Bahji et al., 2019).

text.text: Notably, among 414,299 college students, eating disorder indications were associated with every substance use outcome examined, including cannabis misuse (Qeadan et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Notably, among 414,299 college students, eating disorder indications were associated with every substance use outcome examined, including cannabis misuse <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Qeadan et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Because these findings do not establish direction, two pathways are plausible.
First, cannabis use may promote binge eating, as cannabis directly alters appetite and the reward value of food.

In a randomized placebo-controlled study, for example, oral delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) increased liking and wanting of high-calorie foods and the amount of milkshake consumed (Weltens et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In a randomized placebo-controlled study, for example, oral delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) increased liking and wanting of high-calorie foods and the amount of milkshake consumed <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Weltens et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Further, animal models of binge eating show reduced endocannabinoid and CB1 receptor signaling in the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex (Bourdy & Befort, 2023).
text.formatted: Further, animal models of binge eating show reduced endocannabinoid and CB1 receptor signaling in the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bourdy & Befort, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As such, cannabis may amplify the rewarding pull of palatable food in individuals who are already prone to loss of control.
Second, binge eating may promote cannabis use.
In bingeeating disorder, negative affect and guilt rise before binge episodes and fall afterward (Schaefer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In bingeeating disorder, negative affect and guilt rise before binge episodes and fall afterward <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Schaefer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Distress of this kind may motivate the use of other coping strategies, and many young adults use cannabis to reduce psychological distress (Wallis et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Distress of this kind may motivate the use of other coping strategies, and many young adults use cannabis to reduce psychological distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Wallis et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although cannabis may plausibly intensify binge eating and vice versa, direct evidence in young people is limited.
For example, in a community sample of 1,568 emerging adults, past-year cannabis use was associated with binge eating among women but not men (Elran-Barak et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, in a community sample of 1,568 emerging adults, past-year cannabis use was associated with binge eating among women but not men <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Elran-Barak et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the association among women persisted after adjustment for depressive symptoms.

Further, among 165 treatment-seeking adults with weekly binge eating, about 23% reported cannabis use in the past three months, and cannabis users did not differ from nonusers in eating disorder or depression severity but reported more alcohol use and problems (Wilkinson et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, three questions remain unresolved: 1) how common binge eating is among cannabis-using young adults, 2) whether the association strengthens with frequency of cannabis use, and 3) whether the combination carries more burden than either behavior alone.
College students are an especially informative population for these questions for three reasons.
First, they are concentrated in the window in which both conditions emerge, as emerging adulthood centers on ages 18 to 25 (Arnett, 2000).

text.text: Specifically, cannabis use is highest in this age group and continues to rise (Hinckley et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Specifically, cannabis use is highest in this age group and continues to rise <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Hinckley et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Further, the median age of onset for BED falls in the late teens to early twenties (Kessler et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Further, the median age of onset for BED falls in the late teens to early twenties <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kessler et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Second, both exposures are changing on campuses: eating disorder symptoms increased among US college students from 2013 to 2020 (Romano et al., 2022).

To address these gaps, the current study had four aims.
First, we estimated the prevalence of binge-eating psychopathology among cannabis-using and non-using students.
Second, we tested whether this association strengthens with frequency of cannabis use.
Third, we tested whether the association holds when the binge eating frequency threshold is aligned with the DSM-5 criteria of once weekly (i.e., 4x in the past month).
Fourth, we estimated the burden of co-occurring binge eating and cannabis use on mental health, suicidality, academic functioning, and help-seeking behaviors.
Data comes from ten cohorts (2015-16 to 2024-25) of the Healthy Minds Study (HMS), an annual, web-based survey fielded at participating US colleges and universities (Lipson et al., 2019).

text.text: All respondents completed three core modules, Demographics, Mental Health Status, and Mental Health Survey Utilization/Help Seeking, and up to 10 elective modules chosen by their institution that focus on separate areas of well-being.

We leveraged both the mandatory and elective modules and analyzed variables related to eating behaviors, cannabis and other drug use, mental health, treatment, academic impairment attributed to specific behaviors, and demographic information.

If students indicated that they have recreationally used cannabis products over the past 30 days, they would then be asked the frequency, which is classified into less than once per week, 1-2 days per week, 3-4 days per week, nearly every day, and (nearly) daily.
SCOFF eating disorder screener.
Developed by Morgan et al. in 1999, the SCOFF questionnaire is a widely adopted screening instrument for eating disorders (Morgan et al., 1999).

text.text: Scoring at least a 2 out of 5 on the SCOFF's yes/no questions suggests possible anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa.
Since Bulimia is a diagnostic rule-out for Binge Eating Disorder, adopting the diagnosis-based definition of BED would exclude students who both binge and purge.
Hence, we used loss of control over eating (a "yes" on SCOFF question 2), a subclinical behavioral variable, as the primary exposure, rather than a BN or BED diagnosis.

We also used SCOFF total scores to define the following thresholds: probable eating disorder (aligning with the original SCOFF cutoff; ≥2), HMS positive screen (HMS defines eating disorder as positive at this level; ≥3), and severe (≥4).
The Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q) is a 28question self-report questionnaire that measures the range, frequency, and severity of eating disorder symptoms (Fairburn & Beglin, 1994).
text.formatted: The Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q) is a 28question self-report questionnaire that measures the range, frequency, and severity of eating disorder symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Fairburn & Beglin, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The HMS includes open-ended behavioral frequency questions from the EDE-Q. It asks how many days over the past 28-day period a student experienced an objective binge episode, characterized by an unusually large amount of food and a loss of control over eating.
We defined three levels of severity: ≥1, ≥4 (meeting DSM-5's weekly frequency criterion), and ≥8 (matching DSM-5's criteria for severe BED and/or BN).
Additionally, students were asked the number of times they engaged in each type of compensatory behavior over the past 28 days, including vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, exercise, and fasting.
Depression.
The Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) is a self-report screening questionnaire for depression, developed by Kroenke, Spitzer, and Williams in 1999.
Patients are asked to rate how often they are bothered by 9 core depression symptoms over the past 2 weeks, from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day).
The scores are summed up to 0 to 27, with higher scores indicating more severe symptoms.
We analyzed the continuous scores as well as two binary variables provided in the HMS codebook: a positive depression screen (PHQ-9 ≥ 10) and major depression (PHQ-9≥15).
However, it is important to note that a positive screen is not a diagnosis.
Anxiety.
The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 (GAD-7) is a seven-question screen for generalized anxiety disorder and asks patients how much they are bothered by seven core anxiety problems, rated 0-3.
We analyzed continuous scores and a binary variable for a positive anxiety screen (GAD-7 ≥ 10).
The binary variables suicide ideation, planning, and attempt evaluates whether a student has seriously considered, planned, or attempted taking their own life over the past 12 months.

Non-suicidal self-injury refers to instances where a student hurts themselves on purpose without the intention of killing themselves, which includes but is not limited to cutting, burning, punching or banging themselves, scratching, hair-pulling, biting, interfering with wound-healing, skin-carving, rubbing sharp objects into skin, punching or banging any objects.
In the HMS, students reported how eating and body image concerns affected their academic performance in the past year.

They could select all that apply: did not experience this, experienced this but did not affect academic performance, lower grades on exams and projects, lower grades on courses, incomplete or dropped courses, significant disruption in research, practicum, thesis, or dissertation work, or other.
We coded these into a binary variable: 1 if a student endorsed any of the last five boxes, and 0 if they endorsed only the first two.
Students who were not shown these items are coded as missing.
Help-seeking and care.
We coded 1 if a student reported receiving any clinical mental health treatment (therapy or medication) over the past 12 months, and 0 otherwise.
Untreated distress.
We calculated this as the proportion of students who screened positive for depression or anxiety but did not receive mental health treatment of any kind.
Out-of-range variables were set to NA, which mostly concerned self-report questionnaires and numerical variables.
For example, Binge days was restricted to the 0-28-day range, whereas the purge/fasting variables were not subject to the same restriction, as they asked for the number of occurrences, not days.
Age was restricted to 18-64 years.
Most students were young adults (76.7% weighted; 95% CI [75.7, 77.8]) aged 18-25.
Flourishing scale, PHQ-9, and GAD-7 were restricted to valid scores of 8-56, 0-2, and 0-21 respectively.
Race and gender checkboxes were kept at 0/1, with text versions reconciled later.
The HMS exports "select all that apply" items as 1 or blank.
Thus, for the personal substance use question, a blank cannabis checkbox could mean either that a student saw the list but did not endorse cannabis, or that they were never shown the list.
Treating blanks as "no" would understate the prevalence of cannabis use.
To distinguish these, we counted a response only if at least one item on the list, including the "none of these" option, was checked.
Cannabis use was coded 1 if endorsed and 0 if not endorsed among administered students and set to missing otherwise.
This ensured that students who were not administered the battery were not counted as non-users.
The same rule applied to SCOFF and academic impairment batteries.

text.text: In this pooled sample of more than half a million US emerging adults, binge eating and cannabis use were common and strongly linked.
Specifically, students who used cannabis were more likely to report loss of control over eating than students who did not, and a notable subset of students (8.3%) reported both behaviors.
Importantly, students reporting both also had markedly higher rates of depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts and behavior, self-injury, and academic harm than students with neither.

Because both behaviors were common and the co-occurring group fared clearly worse, the comorbidity is common enough to matter for campus populations and burdensome enough to warrant its own attention.
Key findings are described below.
The patterns observed across levels of cannabis use clarify what this association reflects.

Loss of control over eating was about equally common at every frequency of cannabis use and was lower only among students who did not use cannabis, whereas severe screening results became more common as cannabis use became more frequent.

Taken together, these patterns suggest that any cannabis use is associated with the experience of losing control over one's eating, and that more frequent cannabis use is then associated with more severe eating pathology.
However, given that these analyses are cross-sectional, the direction of these associations cannot be determined.
On the one hand, experimental evidence suggests that cannabis use may increase the reward value of food and thereby the likelihood of losing control while eating (Weltens et al., 2019).
text.formatted: On the one hand, experimental evidence suggests that cannabis use may increase the reward value of food and thereby the likelihood of losing control while eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Weltens et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, students who lose control over eating may turn to cannabis, and those with more severe eating pathology may use it more often if it helps them manage the distress that follows binge episodes (Schaefer et al., 2020; Wallis et al., 2022).
text.formatted: On the other hand, students who lose control over eating may turn to cannabis, and those with more severe eating pathology may use it more often if it helps them manage the distress that follows binge episodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Schaefer et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Wallis et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These two directions are not mutually exclusive and may reinforce one another over time.

Additionally, because the gradient was not perfectly regular (i.e., severe screening results were similar at three to four and one to two days per week), a precise dose-response relationship cannot be inferred.
These findings also help to reconcile earlier studies that reached different conclusions.
Specifically, among treatment-seeking adults who all reported binge eating at least weekly, cannabis use was unrelated to eating disorder severity (Wilkinson et al., 2024).

text.text: Because everyone in that sample binged frequently, the range of severity was restricted, and associations are harder to detect when severity varies so little.

In contrast, our student sample spans the full range of severity (i.e., from no loss of control to severe screening results). Elran-Barak et al. (2025) found an association in women but not men in a community sample.

text.text: While we adjusted for sex at birth, we did not formally test sex differences in this sample.
Thus, sexstratified analyses are a clear next step because the association may differ for women and men.
The EDE-Q subsample strengthens confidence that the association involves behavioral binge eating and not only worry about loss of control over eating as assessed by the SCOFF.
Specifically, weekly binge eating was more common among cannabis users than among nonusers in this subsample, and this difference was statistically significant.
This agreement across measures matters because the SCOFF item captures a cognition and not behavior (Morgan et al., 1999).

text.text: As such, it supports the use of this item as a screen for binge eating in the context of cannabis use.

However, the EDE-Q only approximates the diagnostic threshold because it covers 28 days and the DSM-5 requires three months, and self-report questionnaires can also yield higher binge frequencies than interviews (Fairburn & Beglin, 1994).

text.text: Interview-based assessment is a logical next step for confirming diagnoses.
Several explanations could account for the association between cannabis use and binge eating.
One possibility is that cannabis increases appetite and the reward value of palatable food (Weltens et al., 2019).

text.text: However, this explanation alone cannot account for why severe scores on the SCOFF and loss-of-control eating episodes were also elevated, given that greater appetite does not by itself explain a sense of lost control.
A second possibility involves negative affect, as binge eating is typically preceded by rising negative affect and guilt and followed by improvements in affect (Schaefer et al., 2020).

text.text: As such, cannabis use and binge eating may be two ways of coping with the same distress.

A third possibility is that the two behaviors influence one another over time: adolescent cannabis use has preceded later depression and suicidality (Gobbi et al., 2019), and the resulting distress may in turn maintain binge eating.

text.text: Because our design is cross-sectional, we cannot determine which explanation is correct.
Importantly, each explanation implies a different treatment target (i.e., appetite and reward responses, negative affect and emotion regulation, or both).
The burden associated with co-occurrence was large, which is important because it shows that the combination is more than a statistical overlap.

Notably, students who reported both behaviors were substantially more likely to have attempted suicide in the past year than students who reported neither, and this difference was statistically significant.

This finding is consistent with earlier work in which subthreshold eating disorder symptoms (Lipson & Sonneville, 2020) and adolescent cannabis use (Gobbi et al., 2019) each predicted suicidal ideation and attempts.

text.text: Thus, students who carry both risk factors may be especially vulnerable because each risk factor adds its own pathway to suicidal thoughts and behavior.
We examined interaction on the additive scale because it reflects how many students are affected (Knol & VanderWeele, 2012).
text.formatted: We examined interaction on the additive scale because it reflects how many students are affected <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Knol & VanderWeele, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: On this scale, the excess risk was greater than expected from the two behaviors separately for depression, self-injury, suicidal ideation, and academic harm, and these interactions were statistically significant.

However, because these estimates came from odds ratios and odds ratios overstate risk ratios when outcomes are common, they should be confirmed with models that estimate risk ratios or risk differences.

Students who reported both behaviors were also more likely to be receiving mental health care (i.e., both psychotherapy and psychotropic medication), and these differences were statistically significant.
Further, among students who screened positive for depression or anxiety, those reporting both behaviors were less likely to be untreated.

This pattern likely reflects greater symptom severity in the co-occurring group, given that more severe symptoms tend to prompt help seeking, and it also fits the broader rise in service use among college students (Lipson et al., 2019).

text.text: Because these students are already in contact with campus services, those services are well positioned to identify the comorbidity.
These findings suggest several practical steps.
Clinicians who treat binge eating can routinely ask about cannabis use, and clinicians who address cannabis use can ask about loss of control over eating.
Both questions are warranted because each behavior was associated with the other and either may go unnoticed when only one is assessed.
Further, because loss of control was about equally common at every frequency of cannabis use, even occasional users merit a brief question about binge eating.

Subsequently, trials should test whether integrated treatment outperforms treating either behavior alone, as this is the most direct way to learn whether addressing both behaviors together improves outcomes.
Findings from the current study should be interpreted in light of several limitations.
First, the HMS draws on self-selected campuses and the weights do not adjust for which campuses take part.
As such, prevalence estimates describe students at participating campuses and should not be read as national rates.
Second, all participants were enrolled students and, given that the developmental and campus context may influence both behaviors, generalization to peers outside college requires replication.
Third, no cohort assessed cannabis use disorder.
Because frequency of cannabis use includes many students without impairment, our estimates may understate associations for problematic cannabis use.

Fourth, we did not adjust for tobacco and alcohol use because both are co-used with cannabis and may lie on the causal pathway, and adjusting for them could remove part of the association of interest.
Thus, our estimates are best read as total associations.
Next steps include 1) longitudinal and momentary assessment designs, 2) direct assessment of cannabis use disorder, and 3) tests of whether treating one behavior changes the other.
Longitudinal and momentary designs are particularly critical because they can establish temporal order, which cross-sectional data cannot.
In summary, binge eating among cannabis-using college students is common and linked to a heavy burden of distress.
As such, this comorbidity warrants dedicated attention from researchers and clinicians.
